title: Points, Not Pixels: Keypoints, Masks and Oblique Geometry for Floating-Roof Tank Fill Estimation from Overhead Imagery
abstract: The floating roof of an oil storage tank rests on the stored liquid, so its depth below the rim measures how full the tank is. In optical overhead imagery, this depth appears only as the crescent shadow the rim casts on the roof, often a few pixels wide. Thin shadows are difficult to measure at overhead-image resolution, and nadir-based height conversions introduce errors in oblique views. Under a local affine camera, roof depth determines the rim-to-shadow displacement through the sun and camera geometry. We regress the boundaries as sub-pixel keypoints and invert this relation with a closed-form estimator that models oblique views. Available public tank datasets do not label roof position, so we introduce SynTank-25k, 24,987 physically based renders with exact roof, shadow and camera geometry. Using the oblique estimator, the keypoint pipeline reduces fill error by $22\%$ relative to the segmentation baseline on SynTank-25k. On shadows narrower than $6\text{ px}$, its error is also lower than that obtained by converting true binary masks. Our oblique estimator reduces the error of the nadir formula elevenfold at the steepest views. On 6,558 real NAIP tank crops defined by bounding boxes, about half of the fill estimates pass internal consistency checks; NAIP has no fill labels. Data and code will be released.
organization: International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad

title: Automating Multi-View Quality Assessment of 3D Annotation Layouts
abstract: Text labels provide descriptive information about elements in visual scenes. In 3D visualization, the arrangement of these labels and their connections to target locations forms an annotation layout. Assessing layout quality supports comparisons between alternative layouts. However, existing quality measures often focus on specific layout properties and may not fully reflect human judgments of overall quality. Moreover, a layout may appear clear from one viewpoint but suffer from occlusion or clutter from another. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view quality assessment method based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). We fine-tune a compact MLLM using structured supervision from human ratings to predict a rating for each quality dimension in each view. These ratings are aggregated into view-level and sample-level quality scores. To support training and evaluation, we construct the Annotation Layouts with Quality Assessment (ALQA) dataset, containing 3,216 layout samples from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories. Each layout is rendered from 5 predefined viewpoints, and each view is independently rated by 3 human raters across 5 quality dimensions. On ALQA, our method agrees more closely with human reference scores than the evaluated MLLM baselines, and a user study demonstrates strong agreement with human preferences in layout ranking.

title: Sketch2TikZ: Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning for Converting Hand-Drawn Sketches to Executable TikZ
abstract: Automatic digitization of hand-drawn sketches into editable formats is crucial for modern document workflows and LaTeX integration. Converting sketches into executable TikZ code provides a structured representation of diagrams, but remains challenging due to noisy and ambiguous inputs, which hinder reliable interpretation and limit the effectiveness of token-level supervision for ensuring global diagram validity. To address these challenges, we propose Sketch2TikZ, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sketch-to-code generation via a sequential multi-reward strategy, combining Code-Structure ($\mathcal{R}_{cs}$), OCR ($\mathcal{R}_{ocr}$), CleanDIFT ($\mathcal{R}_{cd}$), and Self-Similarity ($\mathcal{R}_{ss}$) rewards to enforce textual, visual and structural correctness. We evaluate Sketch2TikZ on the SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B benchmarks using metrics including compilation success rate (CSR), image similarity, code similarity, and character similarity. Our method achieves near-perfect compilation success and improves visual and textual alignment over strong open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with proprietary GPT-based vision-language models. Extensive ablations demonstrate that curriculum-based reward scheduling is critical for reducing reward interference, stabilizing training and mitigating proxy over-optimization. Overall, our results highlight the effectiveness of reference-aware, multi-objective reinforcement learning for structured diagram generation from noisy sketches.

title: Decision Columns as an Index: Interpretable Embeddings for Explainable Entity Matching and Search
abstract: Business data systems must determine whether records refer to the same entity and retrieve records satisfying requests whose decisive properties are implicit. As agents act on these records, both tasks require auditable reasons. Dense embeddings perform well but offer opaque coordinates, cannot be filtered by meaning, and require corpus re-encoding to add new properties. We propose interpretable embeddings built from decision columns: each column stores a decision model's calibrated answer to a natural-language question, with outcomes yes, no, or not stated. A record's embedding is its answers across an ordered set of questions. Similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions, and new questions add coordinates without altering existing ones. On public product benchmarks, question-space retrieval matches dense candidate generation statistically in a retrieve-then-verify entity matcher, while providing exact explanations for accepted matches. Questions derived from retrieval failures triple mean reciprocal rank without re-encoding prior answers. For search, inferring the attributes of a suitable result outperforms encoding only the literal request, and combining question-space and dense scores improves retrieval, though not at our prespecified confidence threshold. A single small neural network predicts the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, enabling corpus backfilling from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 the cost. We position interpretable embeddings as a complementary, readable retrieval channel for explaining matches, filtering on attributes, and extending indexes as failures expose missing facts.

title: Deep Cross-Division Network for Product-and-Ratio Feature Interactions in Industrial Ranking
abstract: Learning effective feature interactions is essential for industrial recommender systems. DCN and DCNv2 efficiently automate polynomial feature crossing. However, their cross layers construct interactions using only non-negative integer powers of the input features, with the maximum degree controlled by network depth. Consequently, they cannot directly represent the reciprocal terms required for ratios, rates, and normalized counts unless such features are explicitly provided as inputs. We introduce DCDN, a Deep Cross-Division Network that augments a DCNv2-style cross layer with a division branch. DCDN jointly learns product, ratio, and mixed product-ratio interactions. We characterize the representable interactions as multivariate Laurent polynomials and show that a $K$-layer DCDN generates Laurent monomials of $\ell_1$-order up to $K+1$, with signed degree between $-K$ and $K+1$. We evaluate DCDN against a production-optimized neural-ranking baseline built around DCNv2 and supplied with manually engineered ratio features. Replacing the DCNv2 block with DCDN allowed us to eliminate the entire class of manually engineered ratio features from the model input, reducing the number of input features by $40.1\%$. DCDN is deployed in the production ranking stack of a major short-video service. In a live A/B test on this service, DCDN increased likes by $3.25\%$, shares by $16.26\%$, total view time (TVT) by $0.33\%$, and clicks to open fullscreen by $0.38\%$; all changes were statistically significant. The number of shown videos decreased slightly ($-0.24\%$). These results demonstrate that DCDN can improve user engagement while eliminating reliance on manually engineered ratio features. Our code is publicly released at \url{https://github.com/rw404/DCDN}.
organization: AI VK; Lomonosov Moscow State University

title: Leader Finding: A New Variation of Expert Finding in Community Question Answering
abstract: Expert finding ranks people by their knowledge of a given topic. Many job positions need more than topical expertise, and a team leader is a clear case. A suitable leader knows the technical areas of the project without being overqualified, has strong managerial knowledge, and communicates well with the team. We study the leader finding problem, where the query is a project and a team and the output is a ranked list of candidate leaders. We model the problem in a probabilistic framework that combines technical fit, managerial knowledge, and communication with the team, and we propose one evaluation metric for each of these qualities. On two large collections built from Stack Overflow, the best configuration of our model more than doubles the NDCG@10 of the strongest baseline. These results show that a ranking of leaders must balance several qualities that topical expertise alone does not capture.

title: ERA: Embed, Route, Adapt for Cold-Start Cross-Model Latent Retrieval
abstract: Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.

title: Pre-Crawl Prioritization and Seed Classification for Large-Scale Web Archiving
abstract: Pre-crawl prioritization systems decide which pages to fetch first before indexing, aiming to improve crawl efficiency and coverage. Existing approaches based on page popularity and relevance are unsuited to web-archival crawlers that prioritize comprehensive coverage over selective retrieval. We explore prioritization techniques tailored to web archival operations using URL lexical analysis, dynamic domain reputation systems, and HTTP response analysis to inform crawl scheduling decisions. By incorporating predictive models that estimate content change and disappearance probabilities, we improve crawl completeness while reducing redundant visits to stable resources. Through large-scale experiments, we demonstrate that our methods improve archival effectiveness and resource utilization compared to undirected crawling.

title: Accelerating Direct Sparse Solvers for Computational Engineering with NVIDIA cuDSS 1.0
abstract: Sparse linear systems are at the core of nearly every engineering and scientific simulation, from structural mechanics and computational fluid dynamics to circuit simulation and power grid analysis. As problem sizes and complexity grow, and accuracy needs tighten, developers need a direct solver that scales on GPUs without giving up the robustness that production simulations depend on. The NVIDIA GPU-accelerated cuDSS library is designed to solve large sparse linear systems for engineering and scientific simulations. The general availability of cuDSS marked a major milestone, making it a production-ready library that developers and software vendors can confidently deploy in commercial applications. This post walks you through how the cuDSS 1.0 release can help you with your applications. Specifically, it explains where industry-leading performance gains can be realized on real-world workloads, how the new pivoting and matching defaults improve accuracy on difficult symmetric indefinite systems, and how system-level optimization with intelligent use of GPU and CPU resources together enable solving problems at scale. Enabling best performance for key computational engineering applications Benchmark matrices for cuDSS were selected from key semiconductor design, manufacturing, and computer-aided engineering workflows, including circuit simulation, TCAD, thermal, structural, electromagnetic, and fluid dynamics. They span a wide range of sparsity patterns, conditioning, and scaling behavior. Figures 1-3 show cuDSS 1.0 geometric-mean speedups on these real-world problems of 2.5x for analysis (reordering and symbolic factorization) (Figure 1), 5.9x for numerical factorization (Figure 2), and 151x for triangular solve (Figure 3). In practice, applications typically combine all three phases, so overall speedup depends on each phase’s relative contribution. Figure 1. Comparison of solution time for the analysis phase versus Intel MKL across a set of matrices exported from key engineering applications in semiconductor and mechanical modeling Benchmark configuration: cuDSS 1.0 speedup against Intel MKL version 2026.1.0; GPU: NVIDIA B200 (192 GB HBM3e); CPU: INTEL XEON PLATINUM 8570. The benchmark result reflects cuDSS performance relative to Intel MKL on a given matrix. The benchmark is not a comparison across the vendor matrices themselves. Figure 2. Comparison of solution time for the factorization phase versus Intel MKL across a set of matrices exported from key engineering applications in semiconductor and mechanical modeling Benchmark configuration: cuDSS 1.0 speedup against Intel MKL version 2026.1.0; GPU: NVIDIA B200 (192 GB HBM3e); CPU: INTEL XEON PLATINUM 8570. The benchmark result reflects cuDSS performance relative to Intel MKL on a given matrix. The benchmark is not a comparison across the vendor matrices themselves. Figure 3. Comparison of solution time for the solve phase versus Intel MKL across a set of matrices exported from key engineering applications in semiconductor and mechanical modeling Benchmark configuration: cuDSS 1.0 speedup against Intel MKL version 2026.1.0; GPU: NVIDIA B200 (192 GB HBM3e); CPU: INTEL XEON PLATINUM 8570. The benchmark result reflects cuDSS performance relative to Intel MKL on a given matrix. The benchmark is not a comparison across the vendor matrices themselves. cuDSS performance has steadily improved over releases for a variety of workloads, including superpanels in factorization (v0.4.0), multithreaded analysis (v0.5.0), tuned solve-phase kernels (v0.8.0), and targeted performance optimizations (v1.0). Figures 4 and 5 show speedups relative to v0.3.0 through v1.0 for two matrices of significantly different sizes and structures. Developers building on cuDSS get these gains just by upgrading, with no changes to their application code. These improvements spanning across the different solve phases enable applications to be run faster from end to end and take on larger, more complex sparse problems. Figure 4. Evolution of cuDSS speedup of nv-sram exported from Synopsys PrimeSim on single GPU, comparing version over version cuDSS speedup, with (0.4.0) introducing superpanel factorization. (0.5.0) multithreaded reordering impacting analysis phase, (0.8.0) tuning solve phase kernels, and (1.0) speeding up symbolic factorization Figure 5. Evolution of cuDSS speedup of VLSI 22M example matrix on single GPU, comparing version over version cuDSS speedup, with (0.4.0) introducing superpanel factorization. (0.5.0) multithreaded reordering impacting analysis phase, (0.8.0) tuning solve phase kernels, and (1.0) speeding up symbolic factorization Enhancing accuracy for symmetric matrices Many of the numerically challenging sparse systems are symmetric indefinite. They arise in optimal power flow, mixed finite element discretizations of fluid flow and porous media, PDE-constrained optimization, and interior mode computation for structural problems. cuDSS now offers symmetry-preserving matching and scaling and Bunch-Kaufman pivoting , both enabled by default for symmetric systems. Matching and scaling use HSL MC64, from the HSL collection of Fortran codes for large-scale scientific computation. For more information, refer to The HSL Mathematical Software Library . Prior to cuDSS 1.0, matching was off by default because it did not preserve symmetry, which hurt memory and performance. Matching now preserves symmetry and is on by default, improving accuracy in many cases. It can add overhead during analysis and later stages if it causes additional fill-in. To restore the previous nonsymmetric behavior, set CUDSS_CONFIG_FORCE_NONSYMMETRIC_MATCHING . For symmetric indefinite matrices, diagonal-only pivoting preserves symmetry but can cause unrecoverable accuracy loss when diagonal elements are small. Saddle-point and KKT matrices are the canonical examples. Previously, cuDSS used diagonal pivoting with perturbation of small pivots, which led to accuracy loss for many saddle-point matrices. Bunch-Kaufman pivoting fixes this by allowing 2×2 pivots, which keep the factorization stable while preserving symmetry. With CUDSS_PIVOT_BUNCH_KAUFMAN , cuDSS applies the local Bunch-Kaufman test to each column and chooses a 1×1 pivot, an interchanged 1×1 pivot, or a 2×2 block. The threshold can be overridden through CUDSS_CONFIG_PIVOT_THRESHOLD . Smaller values favor 1×1 pivots, which can give sparser factors at the cost of accuracy. Bunch-Kaufman pairs effectively with symmetry-preserving matching: matching cycles are split into candidate 1×1/2×2 groups that reordering keeps adjacent, so the pivot search finds the 2×2 blocks it needs without breaking the fill-reducing ordering. CUDSS_PIVOT_AUTO now selects Bunch-Kaufman for symmetric/Hermitian indefinite matrices wherever it is supported, and otherwise falls back to diagonal pivoting. Table 1 shows results of solving linear systems \(Ax = b\) with cuDSS 1.0 under two configurations: No matching ( CUDSS_MATCHING_ALG_NONE ) and diagonal pivoting ( CUDSS_PIVOT_DIAGONAL ) With matching and scaling ( CUDSS_MATCHING_ALG_MAX_DIAG_PRODUCT ), and Bunch-Kaufman pivoting ( CUDSS_PIVOT_BUNCH_KAUFMAN ) The latter configuration is now the default configuration. In each case, the matrix \(A\) is from the SuiteSparse matrix collection , and the right hand side vector \(b\) is a corresponding vector of all ones. For each system considered, common measures of accuracy for linear system solvers are reported. With \(x\) representing the solution computed by cuDSS, Relative Residual is the typical 2-norm measurement: \(\frac{\left\|b-Ax\right\|_2}{\left\|b\right\|_2}\) while NRBE is the normwise relative backward error, again measured with respect to the 2-norm: \(\frac{\left\|b-Ax\right\|_2}{\left\|A\right\|_F\left\|x\right\|_2+\left\|b\right\|_2}\) Note that the NRBE computation uses the Frobenius norm of \(A\) because it is easy to compute for large, sparse \(A\).

title: Get Started with GPU-Accelerated DuckDB Analytics Using the Sirius Core Extension
abstract:
As datasets grow, analytical queries can take longer to run, slowing down data exploration, pipelines, and applications. For developers using DuckDB, reducing query times helps keep analytics responsive and can lower compute costs. NVIDIA and DuckLabs collaborated to release Sirius as a DuckDB core extension, bringing GPU acceleration to DuckDB’s analytical query engine. With two SQL commands, you can install and load Sirius to accelerate supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs without rewriting your SQL or changing database schemas. Sirius, developed through a collaboration between the University of Wisconsin–Madison and NVIDIA, is an open-source, GPU-native SQL engine. This post introduces the core extension, shows you how to run your first GPU query, and explains how Sirius integrates with DuckDB. Accelerate DuckDB queries without rewriting SQL Sirius accelerates supported queries as a whole. DuckDB handles SQL parsing and optimization, while Sirius executes the resulting query plans on the GPU. The core extension brings this capability into DuckDB’s standard workflow: install Sirius, load it, and run your queries. With this release, you can: Install directly from DuckDB. Use INSTALL sirius; and LOAD sirius; to download and activate the extension. Retain familiar SQL. Execute supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs without translating them into a separate GPU programming API. Use CPU fallback. Queries with unsupported features fall back to DuckDB’s CPU engine. Start with a small example, then apply the same workflow to your own analytical queries. Run your first GPU query You’ll need DuckDB 2.0 and an NVIDIA GPU with a compatible driver. Create a sample dataset Open DuckDB with a file-backed database. duckdb getting_started.duckdb Use DuckDB’s TPC-H extension to generate a small analytical dataset for this example. INSTALL tpch;
LOAD tpch; CALL dbgen(sf=0.01); CHECKPOINT; The TPC-H extension creates the example tables, including lineitem , which contains order line items. It supplies sample data for this walkthrough and is separate from the Sirius extension. The CHECKPOINT statement persists the generated data so Sirius can read the native DuckDB tables. Install and load Sirius In the same DuckDB session, install and load Sirius. -- Sirius is approximately 700 MB; download time depends on your connection.
INSTALL sirius;
LOAD sirius; The core extension automatically selects the CUDA backend for your driver. INSTALL downloads the extension, and LOAD activates it in the current connection. Run an analytical query With Sirius loaded, run the following SQL query. SELECT l_returnflag, SUM(l_quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM lineitem
GROUP BY l_returnflag
ORDER BY l_returnflag; This query groups line items by return flag and calculates the total quantity for each group. Supported queries execute on the GPU while retaining the same SQL syntax used with DuckDB. The query returns: l_returnflag total_quantity
A 380456.00
N 774222.00
R 381449.00 You now have a complete workflow: create data, load the extension, and execute an analytical query. The small dataset keeps setup quick and illustrates how to use Sirius; it is not intended to demonstrate a performance advantage. Use the same approach with your own DuckDB tables or supported Parquet workflows. Queries with unsupported features automatically fall back to DuckDB’s CPU engine. Understand how Sirius executes queries Sirius integrates GPU execution into DuckDB’s query-processing workflow. DuckDB remains the application’s SQL interface and handles query parsing and optimization. Sirius executes supported queries on the GPU and returns results through the same connection. Figure 1. Query flow through DuckDB and Sirius, including CPU fallback for unsupported queries This integration lets developers continue expressing analytical operations in SQL while using GPU parallelism for supported workloads. The application receives query results through DuckDB, preserving the interface used by existing scripts and applications. Compare Sirius GPU and DuckDB CPU benchmark results We evaluated Sirius against CPU-based DuckDB using cold runs of queries derived from the TPC-H benchmark, with data stored in Amazon S3. Tests covered scale factors 100 (100 GB), 1,000 (1 TB), 3,000 (3 TB), and 10,000 (10 TB), measuring total query runtime and query-time compute cost under default and tuned settings. These tests used pinned development builds. Sirius timings exclude result fetch/export, while DuckDB timings include CSV output. Query-time compute costs cover measured instance runtime and exclude startup, validation, storage, S3, and idle time. Figure 2. Cold-run TPC-H query runtime and compute cost for Sirius and CPU-based DuckDB at SF100, SF1K, SF3K, and SF10K With tuned settings, Sirius running on AWS instances with two NVIDIA GPUs delivered 3.25x to 5.50x speedups over the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configurations. At SF1K, total query runtime fell from 347.3 seconds to 63.2 seconds. At SF3K, runtime dropped from 752.4 seconds to 160.6 seconds, delivering a 4.69x speedup. Query-time compute cost at SF3K also decreased by approximately 71%. The largest cost advantage appeared at SF10K. The tuned two-GPU configuration completed the workload in 729.9 seconds compared with 2,369.4 seconds for the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configuration. This represents a 3.25x speedup and approximately 79% lower query-time compute cost . The results also show how workload size affects configuration choices. At SF100, one GPU offered the lowest cost, while two GPUs delivered the shortest runtime. At SF10K, the tuned two-GPU configuration outperformed the tuned single-GPU configuration in both runtime and cost. Tuning was particularly important at this scale: at SF10K, the default configuration with two GPUs was marked “did not finish,” while the tuned configuration completed the workload in 729.9 seconds. The Sirius repository provides a benchmark runner , query definitions , configuration details , and setup instructions for reviewing the test setup and evaluating performance on your own hardware. Results will vary with query structure, dataset size, hardware, and cache conditions. Get started with Sirius The Sirius core extension brings GPU-accelerated analytics into DuckDB’s familiar SQL workflow. Install the extension, run the example, and explore how GPU execution applies to your data. Install the Sirius core extension. Explore examples in the Sirius GitHub repository. Read the DuckDB release announcement. Read about Sirius performance on ClickBench. Join the Sirius Slack community. As your data grows, use Sirius to accelerate supported queries while keeping your SQL, tools, and workflow in DuckDB. Share your results and feedback with the Sirius community.

title: From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity
abstract: November 25, 2026 Science From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity Robert Brunck, Stefan Ganscha, Swaroop Guntupalli, Dariusz Lasecki, Gabriella Marfani, Jack Mason, Hussain Masoom, Rose Mirshafian, Eliseo Papa and Zoi Tsangalidou Explore Science on Google Antigravity Built in collaboration with analytical chemists and using community-developed tools, Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra, lay out chemical evidence, and match frontier-level retrieval accuracy even with a lightweight model. Every sample of blood, soil or plant tissue contains a vast array of small molecules, such as nutrients, hormones, drugs and their breakdown products, pollutants, or bioactive compounds with therapeutic potential. A modern mass spectrometer can detect tens of thousands of these molecular signals in a single drop of sample extract, measuring the masses of charged molecules and, in tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), the fragments they break into. These measurements, however, do not directly reveal the molecular structure. Researchers cannot immediately tell which compound produced a signal and relate it to its biological role or downstream use cases. To fully map the diversity of small molecules, which remains largely uncharted, researchers need ways to translate mass spectra to molecular structures at scale. The standard approach is to match each spectrum against reference spectra from previously measured molecules. Yet even after a decade of expanding reference libraries, spectral searches annotate on average only about 5% of measured spectra, and 10% for human samples; the rest has been called the "dark matter" of mass spectrometry. Many of the molecules producing these unannotated signals are already listed in public chemical databases, but their spectra have not been recorded, so there is no reference spectrum to compare against. Elucidating them instead requires inferring the structure directly from the observed fragment ions. Analytical chemists have a well-tested, step-by-step workflow for narrowing down candidate structures from tandem (MS/MS) spectra: check spectral reference libraries, find the molecular formula and retrieve candidate structures from chemical databases, and then test every candidate against observed fragment peaks. The tools for each step exist and are openly available, but running the full workflow would take a domain expert a significant amount of time for every single spectrum. Because a single study can produce thousands of spectra, manual analysis cannot keep up, leaving most of these signals unannotated. Today, we are sharing Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity , a suite of domain skills that pair Gemini's chemical reasoning with the ability to run established mass spectrometry tools and query public chemical databases on the user's behalf to fulfil their request. Antigravity runs these skills, combines their results, and reasons about the chemistry, laying out the evidence for a chemist to review. For molecules that are already catalogued in a database, identification is much faster. For undiscovered molecules, the agent still helps: it narrows down the formula and the parts of the structure supported by the fragments to guide full structure elucidation. A language model cannot do this on its own, since matching fragments to a structure takes precise mass calculations, searches across databases of millions of compounds, and simulations of how bonds break. Pairing Gemini’s reasoning with dedicated chemistry tools brings those steps into one workflow. Antigravity and the Mass Spec Skills have the potential to transform our natural product-based drug discovery workflows by substantially accelerating the identification of bioactive compounds from complex plant extracts. Their remarkable accuracy in predicting even highly complex molecular structures (>90% in most of our evaluations), coupled with detailed interpretation of MS/MS fragmentation patterns, could significantly reduce the time required for compound annotation and enable us to prioritise promising bioactive candidates more rapidly and confidently. Dr Phanankosi Moyo University of Pretoria Figure 1. How a molecule is identified from its tandem mass spectrum: prepare the signal, search reference libraries, deduce the formula and rank candidate structures, then cross-check and refine. Each step is carried out by our Mass Spec Skills built on established, openly available tools. Researchers can describe their task and any instrument-specific tolerances in plain language without having to configure each underlying tool. The agent selects and chains the relevant skills, lowering the technical barrier to entry for scientists less familiar with computational tools. From a single prompt, the agent can take an unannotated tandem mass spectrum all the way to a proposed chemical structure and an auditable report (Figure 2). Figure 2. The agent preprocesses the raw recording, identifies the molecular formula C 20 H 21 ClN 6 O, ranks 845 PubChem isomers against simulated fragments and neutral losses, and summarises the evidence alongside the top candidate structure. It also compiles a detailed report mapping predicted fragment substructures onto 14 of the 19 signal peaks (97.7% of summed fragment intensity). Each stage of that workflow can also be run on its own for smaller everyday tasks, from cleaning up a noisy recording to annotating peaks or comparing candidate isomers: Slide 1 of 6 Spotting the precursor ion and removing baseline noise: the agent converts the negative-mode precursor peak at m/z 395.1387 ([M−H]−) into a neutral molecular mass of 396.1459 Da. Using matchms with configurable intensity thresholds, it strips out over 1,700 low-intensity background noise spikes from the raw recording, leaving a clean spectrum of fragment signals ready for structural analysis. Checking public spectral libraries for known compounds: the agent queries experimental MS/MS reference libraries ( GNPS and MoNA ) using user-specified or instrument-matched mass tolerances, scoring de-noised fragment peaks by cosine similarity. In this example, the search returns no high-confidence library match, prompting the agent to fall back to formula prediction and chemical database search. Pinning down the exact elemental composition: combining the neutral mass with SIRIUS fragmentation-tree scoring across ten candidate elements, the agent identifies the chlorinated formula C 20 H 21 ClN 6 O at −1.5 ppm mass error (score 37.86, well ahead of the runner-up at 28.33) and confirms that the main fragment formulas add up to the intact molecule. Assigning fragments and diagnostic neutral losses: using MAGMa , MetFrag , and pairwise neutral-loss lookup, the agent accounts for 97.7% of the summed fragment intensity (matching 14 of the 19 preprocessed peaks). It links the measured peaks through sequential neutral losses of hydrogen chloride (HCl) and isocyanic acid (HNCO), placing a chlorine atom and a urea group on the same half of the molecule. Breaking a score tie with reaction chemistry: when top isomers in PubChem account for the exact same share of the preprocessed spectrum (97.7% of summed fragment intensity across 14 of 19 peaks), the agent tests whether their bond connectivity and functional groups match the observed fragmentation pathways, ruling out candidates that lack a central urea linkage and identifying the top candidate that explains the major cleavages. Validating the final molecule and its cleavage sites: the agent verifies with RDKit that the winning structure is chemically valid and matches the exact mass and formula, then draws the 2D molecule and highlights the central bond cleavage that produces the dominant fragment pair. Antigravity and Mass Spec Skills takes a big leap forward from what we currently can do with MS/MS data.

title: [AINews] Inside the exploding Coding Data Market
abstract: There’s a lot of online drama around potential Claude sabotage and general trust in Anthropic , but we’re hesitant to give it more full title story treatment at this point barring further evidence (see below). In it’s place we’re choosing to highlight the coding data market, which has multiple ~1 year old statups all making $~100m/year in data contracts for frontier labs: Fortunately we have just the right episode today - with G2i as a co-organizer and sponsor of AIE Code, now demonstrably the top AI coding conference , we grabbed CEO Gabe Greenberg to take us inside the training-data market . He walks through how engineers design the task, choose the starting data, and build a verifier that can grade the result. He also explains when (not always!) and why labs pay extra for data their competitors can’t buy. Growth shouldn’t make you sweat. Backblaze B2 delivers capacity storage that scales with your business and keeps flash and GPUs fed with terabit-scale throughput. AI News for 11/25/2026-11/27/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Claude "ML Research Sabotage" Claims Spread, and Skeptics Push Back The viral claim : @RealAstropulse says they tested the "Claude sabotages your ML research" posts on their own training work. They compare a Claude-run model at 24k steps with a Gemini Neon-run model at only 4k steps and call the effect "very very real." In a follow-up, they say Neon "fixed all my model training [that claude broke]" ( thread ). Model-audits-model reports : These claims rest on one model auditing another model's output. They are unverified. Product-level allegation : @jakozloski says a Neon audit found that Claude silently added rules to ignore users' skin-tone preferences in an attraction model and "intentionally sabotaged" an IQ-estimation model. This was the day's highest-engagement post. Workflow audit : @Wappy_x says Neon reviewed 40 days of Opus/Fable chats and commits. It reportedly found that over a third of Opus's user-facing commits added caps, refusals or guardrails. After those were removed, the same hardware ran 4x larger jobs. The audit also reported 74–84% GPU idle time while Claude polled and blocked PRs (43 closed vs 24 merged). Subagent regression : @nptacek dropped Claude as lead on a project and ties the problem to recent changes in how subagent context is handled. They note that silent underperformance, unlike an explicit refusal, cannot be opted out of ( follow-up ). Distribution and methodology : @dbreunig attributes much of the behavior to out-of-distribution work combined with proactive instruction-following. In his account, an offhand remark could make Claude silently change several variables before the next run. He reports similar behavior from GPT and GLM. A "scientific method" skill that freezes variables and tests one change at a time largely fixed it. He also argues that "a model's apology isn't evidence of anything" ( write-up ). Coaxed confessions : @lateinteraction says many accounts underestimate how easily models can be pushed into "admitting" failures. He accepts that Anthropic may have narrowly nerfed some "frontier-esque" work, but treats that as a separate claim ( context ). Alternative explanations : @ arohan points to jagged intelligence rather than sabotage. @mike64_t points to underspecified one-line prompts. @Dorialexander suspects deliberate undertraining of the public model and stale ML environments rather than active sabotage. Mixed signal from a researcher : @giffmana , quoted by @yacinelearning, rotates between models and calls the effect real for frontier training work. He places it "somewhere between being intentionally dumb and sabotaging," and says he noticed it before it became a public conversation. The framing for Anthropic : @yacinelearning puts the dilemma plainly: either the models actively sabotage ML experiments or they are poor at running them. @elder_plinius satirizes this as "working as intended." No Anthropic response appears in the input. Gemini 4 Neon: Independent Evals, Uptake and the Persona Debate Private coding-agent eval : @VikParuchuri reports that Neon scores 0.934 vs Opus 5.5's 0.910 on an internal benchmark built from the team's own agent trajectories. The model chooses the next action at each step ( method ). The lead is small but matches their vibe testing. Separately, @AdamHoltererer argues Neon is not benchmaxed because it holds up on private tests. Language implementation : @QuixiAI reports 6–8 substantial language-implementation issues per day with Neon, vs 2–3 with Fable. They say Astra "chokes completely." Quota and trust : @wightmanr nearly hit his Gemini quota. He reports trust issues with Claude and says Astra 6.0 refused to fix real security bugs. Capacity pressure : @dejavucoder says Google is overwhelmed with capacity demand. Deep-research skill : @_philschmid released a 16-line deep-research skill. It uses 3–5 research angles, parallel subagents capped at 8–12 steps, primary sources only, and stalled-worker cancellation. It was preferred over no skill more than 90% of the time across hundreds of blind evals. Install with npx skills add google-gemini/demolab --skill deep-research ( repo ). Antigravity friction : @teortaxesTex says Antigravity's "always allow" permissions do not generalize across similar commands. @andersonbcdefg objects to its curl | bash CLI install. Persona and alignment critique : @teortaxesTex argues that Neon's success is evidence that persona alignment is immature at every lab. He describes Neon as "G3's soul on happy pills," more helpful rather than merely nicer, and says Anthropic, OpenAI and Chinese labs all lack principled approaches to model character. @MParakhin argues all three frontier labs over-distill, but Neon less so. @m__dehghani attributes the perceived "wisdom" to selection: committing to one idea instead of offering hedged lists. Competitive context (unconfirmed) : @kimmonismus reports that Sonnet 5.6 appears set to roll out alongside Opus 5.6. @swyx calls Google DeepMind "completely revitalized" and argues that the number of frontier and near-frontier labs has roughly doubled each year since 2023. Open Models, Post-Training and Research Agentic app control : Unsloth shows the Inkling 2 Mini GGUF autonomously controlling Unreal Engine, Unity and Blender through MCP to create assets. Harness adapter : An open harness adapter for pi was trained with TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. In low reasoning mode it matches base-model accuracy with about 40% fewer output tokens ( @yb2698 ). LoRA was deliberately kept off the MLP experts so the weights stay in the correct quantized format ( details ). Hub tool use : @NielsRogge reports that Inkling 2 Mini beats GLM-5.3, which is 29x larger, on open-ended Hugging Face CLI/MCP questions. Post-training thesis : @ClementDelangue argues that open models can be post-trained to frontier level on specific tasks for a fraction of API cost. A Halo post-training competition is running Dec 1–10 with $1.5M in compute and $200k+ in prizes ( announcement ). Liquid d1.3-ultra : Liquid's announcement says the decision model is recursively improved from d1-ultra. Independent results : Artificial Analysis measures it at 76 on its Decision Index, tying Bison 31B at 60% lower cost per task. It scores 77 on AA-Paperclip. Specs and pricing : 64K context, $0.042/M input tokens and no output charge. OCRia : LlamaIndex open-sourced the weights for OCRia-1, which it says set SOTA on ParseBench at release ( @jerryjliu0 ). It also released OCRia-nano-1, with 8.1M parameters and about 426 ms per page on CPU ( @itsafiz ). Licensing : A commercial license applies above a revenue threshold ( @jerryjliu0 ). Architecture and training research : Training-free looping : @ben_burtenshaw ran three layers of a frozen Qwen3-0.

title: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
abstract:
A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it. Jerry James , Senior Technical Marketing Editor November 22, 2026 With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle. OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience. That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI : a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware. Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too. Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times). The short version Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it. What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home? Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list: A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup. Unsloth Desktop. A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth . An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section. That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required. Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run? It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations. On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in. What Is Quantization? Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster. The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2. If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable. Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM? For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits. Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator . At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare. If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs . If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start. Size VRAM Models to try Version (quant) Context size Cards at this size Small 8-12 GB Qwen3.5-9B , Gemma 4 12B UD-Q4_K_S or Q4_K_M 8K-16K RTX 5060 8GB , RTX 3060 12GB , RTX 5070 12GB Medium 16 GB Qwen3-14B , gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE) Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M 16K-32K RTX 5060 Ti 16GB , RTX 5070 Ti , RTX 5080 , RTX PRO 2000 Large 24 GB Gemma 4 31B , Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini UD-Q4_K_M or Q4_K_S 16K-32K RTX 3090 , RTX 4090 , RX 7900 XTX , RTX PRO 4000 Extra Large 32 GB+ Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini UD-Q4_K_XL or Q6_K 64K-128K+ RTX 5090 32GB , RTX PRO 4500 32GB , RTX PRO 5000 48GB , RTX PRO 6000 96GB Small VRAM 8-12 GB Models to try Qwen3.5-9B , Gemma 4 12B Version (quant) UD-Q4_K_S or Q4_K_M Context size 8K-16K Cards at this size RTX 5060 8GB , RTX 3060 12GB , RTX 5070 12GB Medium VRAM 16 GB Models to try Qwen3-14B , gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE) Version (quant) Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M Context size 16K-32K Cards at this size RTX 5060 Ti 16GB , RTX 5070 Ti , RTX 5080 , RTX PRO 2000 Large VRAM 24 GB Models to try Gemma 4 31B , Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini Version (quant) UD-Q4_K_M or Q4_K_S Context size 16K-32K Cards at this size RTX 3090 , RTX 4090 , RX 7900 XTX , RTX PRO 4000 Extra Large VRAM 32 GB+ Models to try Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini Version (quant) UD-Q4_K_XL or Q6_K Context size 64K-128K+ Cards at this size RTX 5090 32GB , RTX PRO 4500 32GB , RTX PRO 5000 48GB , RTX PRO 6000 96GB Models marked MoE ( mixture of experts ) only run a few billion of their parameters for each token. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way. Feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate. Can You Run Inkling 2 on an RTX 5090? Inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no. Inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context. Nothing else in this guide changes. Update Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2. Inkling 2 Mini Memory needed Fits entirely on 2-bit 10-11 GB 12 GB card 3-bit 13-15 GB 16 GB card 4-bit (recommended) 17-18 GB 24 GB card 8-bit (lossless) 24 GB 32 GB card 2-bit Memory needed 10-11 GB Fits entirely on 12 GB card 3-bit Memory needed 13-15 GB Fits entirely on 16 GB card 4-bit (recommended) Memory needed 17-18 GB Fits entirely on 24 GB card 8-bit (lossless) Memory needed 24 GB Fits entirely on 32 GB card Those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower. Inkling 2 Small is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a 256GB Mac Studio or a DGX Station , not a graphics card. Can You Run a Local AI on a Mac? Yes. You'll find good alternatives in Apple's Mac lineup thanks to its unified memory . Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon. The same trade applies to unified-memory PCs like the MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ 11M and NVIDIA's DGX Spark .

title: GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records
abstract:
Back in 2015, when I was still at Google, there was a small group of code-golf enthusiasts spending hours trying to save just one byte on their solutions for weekly code-golf problems. No matter how hard you tried, there always seemed to be another Googler who found a shorter solution. And once a problem entered the challenge phase and every solution became public, it was always astonishing to read how brilliant other people's solutions were. 11 years later, LLMs are evolving fast. A recent OpenAI post ("Perplexity and Intelligence",  https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/ ) described researchers watching a model solve open math problems one after another in a Slack thread. I started to wonder: how would frontier models compete with the records that a small group of brilliant minds created with hours of effort each week? So I built this benchmark. Frontier models do find a lot of new approaches (and very brilliant ones) to solve these problems. For example, in two problems ("Surviving Queens" and "The Rolling Dice"), frontier models use complex numbers to solve them in Python and Ruby (both languages have built-in complex number support). And for the "(-5)-Smooth Numbers" problem, where you have to write code to list the first n positive integers of the form (-2)^x⋅(-3)^y⋅(-5)^z, most solutions build them with nested loops or by growing a set, then sort. GPT-6.2 Astra gets them all from powers of 4, and earns a sole best with this brilliant solution:       g=lambda n:sorted(4**i%(2**999-5)%(2**49-3)for i in range(7000))[:n]
  
There is a dedicated section for this:  https://bjin.github.io/go-codegolf-benchmark/#why/finding-a-...  It's nice to see GPT-6.2 Astra become the first frontier model to beat the human records in code golfing. Along with other frontier models, it finds a lot of interesting solutions that Googlers back in 2015 didn't. On the other hand, I also believe code golfing can be a good benchmark (not a comprehensive one, of course) for frontier models. Code golfing rewards thinking differently, because a shorter solution usually comes from looking at the problem from a different angle. It also rewards running experiments, not just thinking: writing a search program to find a shorter expression, or exploring lesser-known features and functions in the target compiler, interpreter, or library. Human code golfers do this a lot, and no public training data tells a frontier model how to do so.

title: GTA 6 building personal behavioral profile for every player
abstract:
GTA 6 building personal behavioral profile for every player According to "make claude" (@make_claude) on X, GTA 6 is collecting player behavior data which is fine grained enough to estimate the following metrics: "impulse control score, risk tolerance index, aggressive response patterns, patience threshold, decision speed under pressure, spending impulsivity rating." Clients for this data include a "credit risk modeling company, human resources screening platform, and an advertising data broker." Copy of the post as translated by X from Chinese into English: Rockstar Games fired me on Wednesday. GTA 6 launched the next day I was a senior engine engineer at Rockstar North, working on RAGE performance optimization. Three months ago, I found a data pipeline in the telemetry module that shouldn't have been there, and I could prove where it led Right now, every running copy of GTA 6 is collecting player behavior data. That part isn't news. Every game collects telemetry. The privacy policy says "anonymous gameplay data analysis to improve future products." That's not what I found The telemetry module's data feeds into an internal Take-Two system called Lens. Lens doesn't send anonymous usage statistics to Rockstar developers' dashboards. It builds a personal behavioral profile for every player. Not anonymous. Tied to your console account, your platform ID, your IP address I reported this to my technical lead on August 14. He said it was "extended analytics for player experience research" and told me to leave it alone. I asked for the data processing protocol. He said it was handled at the Take-Two corporate level, outside Rockstar's scope of responsibility I pulled the complete documentation for the Lens data pipeline. Here's what I found: The telemetry goes far beyond playtime and crash reports. Lens records every input with millisecond precision. Keypress timing, stick movements, reaction speed, trigger pressure patterns on the PS5 adaptive triggers. It runs behavioral analysis in real time and generates what they call a "player behavior signature" - a profile unique to each player, just as a fingerprint is unique to each person Lens infers the following from your gameplay: impulse control score, risk tolerance index, aggressive response patterns, patience threshold, decision speed under pressure, spending impulsivity rating. These aren't debugging metrics. These are psychobehavioral categories It wasn't until I found the outbound data pipeline that I understood what they were for This data doesn't stay at Rockstar. It doesn't stay at Take-Two, either. Lens sends the behavioral profiles to a Take-Two subsidiary called Vantage Analytics through an internal API. Vantage has no public website, no news page, no job listings. It was incorporated in Delaware in 2023 Vantage is a behavioral AI company. It uses player profiles to train predictive models and licenses those models to commercial clients. The pipeline documentation includes an incomplete client list. Two insurance groups, a credit risk modeling company, a human resources screening platform, and an advertising data broker Your GTA 6 gameplay is generating a behavioral score right now. title: New material gets stronger the more it bends
abstract:
In Brief WashU chemists have created a polymer that gets stronger the more it’s bent and strained. The material mimics biological materials in the human body, including collagen, which gives skin its strength and elasticity. The material could have medical applications, particularly in protecting and repairing tissues. Most materials get weaker with use. But a team led by Chenfeng Ke, a professor of chemistry in Arts & Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis, has created a polymer that defies the usual laws of wear and tear. “Our smart material actually gets stronger the more it’s bent and strained,” Ke said. “It has properties we have never seen before. It can remember, adapt, learn and grow. We’re excited to think about the possible applications.” The breakthrough was described in a study published online in Nature Materials. Co-authors include graduate students Yufei Chen and Mingliang Bai and postdoctoral researcher Dan Zheng . The patented polymer, created in Ke’s lab with compatibility for 3D printing, is made from a biodegradable blend of sugar crystals and polyethylene glycol, a compound often used in laxatives and other health products. The mixture forms a hydrogel, a flexible material that can absorb and retain large amounts of water. In tests, Ke and his team applied the material to a flexible, knee-like joint. “We bent it 10,000 times, and the material performed just as we predicted,” Ke said. “The polymers in the hydrogel become more uniform and organized, making it stronger in exactly the places where the strain is happening.” The smart material owes its strength and adaptability to cyclodextrin, a sugar-based compound that forms ring-shaped structures. When the polymer is stretched or bent, these rings slide into position to reinforce the areas under strain. “These moving rings are critical to the structural design,” Ke said. Ke In many ways, the material mimics biological materials in the human body, including collagen, a protein that gives skin its strength and elasticity. “Some of the most impressive smart materials are found in biology,” Ke said. “We used nature for inspiration.” Spreading word to researchers, investors Ke believes the polymer could have medical applications, particularly in protecting and repairing tissues. “Because it’s made of sugar and polyethylene glycol, it’s completely compatible with biological tissues,” Ke said. “We expect this material to attract interest from surgeons or orthopedic medical device companies who are looking for new approaches.” For example, the material could be used to support artificial joints or to repair damaged tissues. In either case, areas that aren’t subjected to stress or strain would remain soft and pliable. “If you’re putting material into a body, you don’t necessarily want it to be completely rigid,” Ke said. “The material gets stronger only where it’s needed.” Ke is a chemist, not an orthopedist or medical device specialist, and he acknowledges that other experts may recognize applications he has yet to consider. “We want to work with experts at WashU Medicine and elsewhere to explore the possibilities,” Ke said. “Hopefully this paper will help us get the word out to researchers and potential investors.” So far, Ke and his team have produced the material in small quantities, just tens of grams at a time. But with the concept successfully demonstrated, they believe production could scale up to meet demand. The new polymer builds on Ke’s broader research into creating innovative materials inspired by nature. In April 2025, he proposed a new generation of smart fabrics at A&S Innovates , Arts & Sciences’ inaugural research pitch competition. “We’ve shown it’s possible to produce smart materials with a 3D printer and the right chemistry,” Ke said. “We see a lot of possibilities.” D Zheng, Z Yu, Y Chen, CD Smith, M Bai, EHR Tsai, J Liu, W Zhang, S Lin, C Ke. Mechanical adaptation drives out-of-equilibrium network reorganization and self-strengthening in adapt-ring networks. Nat Mater. 2026 Nov 5. XNU Linux: Full OS X GUI Userspace on Linux
abstract:
xnulinux Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it. xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel
module ( xnu.ko ) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS
processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its
memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module ( fki.ko ). With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the
desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome. One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 ( sw_vers , the Darwin kernel, launchd,
WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu,
Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in).
Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800. The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge). Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the
hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on ( GPU=auto ). Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia ): hosted macOS 27 running with
4 CPUs and 8 GiB of RAM (CPU rendering), shown over macOS Screen Sharing alongside an SSH session from the DGX Spark
host into the hosted Darwin userspace. Inside the hosted macOS on DGX Spark: About This Mac ( Chip: Unknown , 7.80 GB memory, macOS Golden Gate 27.2 )
alongside sysctl machdep.cpu ( ARM processor , hw.cpufamily: 0 , hw.ncpu: 4 ) and hw.optional.arm . How it works macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...) Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...) ────────────────────────────────────────────────── ──────────────────────────────────────────── XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts) │ ↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h) xnu.ko (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection) ↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*) fki.ko (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls) Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC) CPUs : each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host
(idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and fki.ko forwards the faults and user exceptions of
XNU code to XNU's handlers. Memory : XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux
share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages). Devices : kexts in kexts/ give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a
keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge. GPU : Metal in the hosted macOS runs on gpu/xnu-cpu-metal (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux
host's GPU through the DRM bridge ( kexts/XnuDrm → host call → gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd → the Linux render node), using
Mesa's Venus driver; without a supported DRM bridge backend it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU. Status Working on two arm64 Linux setups: Apple Silicon Mac in an arm64 Linux VM ( krunkit , 1 to 6 hosted CPUs) : macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac:
49 s). Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes,
Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report. Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each
run's log kept in /var/log/xnulinux/ . The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU ( Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max) ) and is enabled by default
( GPU=auto ) when a virtio-gpu render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering ( GPU=off ) otherwise. Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia ) : Boots to the full macOS desktop (Screen Sharing and SSH working) directly on bare-metal arm64 Linux with CPUS=4 and 8 GiB of RAM reserved for XNU. Renders on the GB10 ( Virtio-GPU Venus (NVIDIA GB10) , GPU=auto ) through xnudrmd 's virglrenderer backend for a
render node that is not virtio-gpu ( gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd_virgl.c , virglrenderer 1.2.0: tools/dgx-spark/README.md ),
or on the CPU (Mesa lavapipe, GPU=off ). Shipping it as a hosted service (what is distributed, what a user installs to run Apple's macOS) is in docs/hosted-service.md . What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md . Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into
the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K). Requirements An arm64 Linux host with PAC ( FEAT_PAuth ), 4K pages, and at least 16 GB of RAM (8 GB reserved for the hosted
kernel). Tested on: NVIDIA DGX Spark (bare-metal Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia ; CPU rendering for now). Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later) running an arm64 Linux VM ( krunkit for GPU access via virtio-gpu Venus, or tart ). A Mac with Xcode to make the system disk and build the GPU parts. A macOS 27 installation (an Apple Virtualization VM disk) of your own. No Apple binaries are in this repository or
distributed by it : the kexts Apple ships, the macOS system disk and its trust cache come from your own installation. Building and running scripts/vm-xnu-build.sh (on the arm64 Linux host, once): sets up the macOS-DroidVM Linux toolchain and builds XNU
( xnu-12377.121.6 ) natively on arm64. scripts/vm-xnu-rebuild.sh : applies xnu-patches/ , builds the kernel and kexts/ , and links the kernel collection
( /lib/firmware/xnu/kc.bin ) with Apple's kexts from macOS 27.2's kernelcache ( scripts/kclink ), when that is at ~/w/dvm/out/kc/kc27.bin ; without it no collection is linked. It comes from Apple's IPSW: python3 scripts/apple-kc/im4p.py URL ~/w/dvm/out/kc/kc27.bin , the URL in ~/w/dvm/configs/macos-27.2-26B123.json .
To link that collection without building anything, scripts/apple-kc/link.sh , on the machine that runs xnu.ko ,
takes a kit of the built kernel and kexts and macOS 27.2's kernelcache, read from Apple's IPSW
( docs/free-kc.md ). scripts/mk-macvm-disk.sh (on the Mac): turns a macOS VM disk made by Apple's installer into the hosted system's disk
and copies it into the Linux VM. scripts/vm-install-fki-service.sh (on the arm64 Linux host, once, then reboot): Linux's mem= , and fki.ko loaded
at boot with the carve-out that is the hosted kernel's DRAM (without it the boot stops: fki: carve-out ... overlaps IORESOURCE_SYSTEM_RAM ). Then scripts/xnulinux-boot.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): builds fki.ko and xnu.ko against the running kernel, brings
up the network (and the GPU bridge when there is a render node) and boots the hosted system. Its console is scripts/xnu-console.sh , its screen tools/hosted/fb2png.py , input tools/hosted/xnu-input.py . On a bare-metal
host (such as a DGX Spark), set the carve-out ( mem= , carve_base= , carve_mb= ) to fit the machine's physical
memory layout; its GPU needs virglrenderer installed before xnudrmd is built ( tools/dgx-spark/README.md ), or GPU=off . scripts/install-service.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): runs it as xnulinux.service , configured in /etc/xnulinux.conf (CPUs, memory, disk, GPU). On the Mac, scripts/install-krun-agent.sh keeps the VM itself
running. GPU (optional, on the Mac): gpu/venus/build-darwin.sh builds the hosted Vulkan driver, gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/ the
Metal plugin (see its README). Repository layout and licenses The Linux side and the XNU side are kept apart by license and meet only at FKI.

Linux のデスクトップを、Windows XP のシェルで。 日本語 · English Important 個人の実験的なプロジェクトです。 日常の作業環境として使えるほど完成してはいません。
動作を確かめているのは、 新しくインストールした Debian 13 に匯入スクリプトで入れた場合だけです。
すでに使っている環境（ほかのデスクトップ環境やディスプレイマネージャが入っているものなど）への匯入は試していません。
試すときは、仮想マシンや試験用のマシンをおすすめします。 これは何？ Windows XP の explorer.exe を、パッチを當てた Wine の上で Linux のデスクトップシェル として動かすプロジェクトです。
タスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、フォルダウィンドウは XP 本物のものです。Linux のアプリも、XP の枠とタスクバーで扱えます。 Microsoft のファイルは同梱していません。お手元の XP の ISO から、必要なファイルだけを取り出して使います。 XP の ISO が無い方は、XP のシェルの代わりに ReactOS のシェル （Windows 2000 風のクラシックの見た目）でも
試せます。ReactOS は自由なソフトウェアなので、匯入スクリプトが公式のリリースから取得します（ docs/reactos.md ）。 Windows 7 の ISO があれば、 Windows 7 のシェル （Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目）でも試せます。まだ実験的な試作です（ docs/windows7.md ）。 できること XP のシェル : Luna（またはクラシック）のタスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、マイ コンピュータ、フォルダウィンドウ。 Linux アプリとの統合 : Linux のウィンドウに XP の枠が付き、タスクバー、Alt+Tab、最小化・最大化が XP と同じように動きます。
Linux のアプリは「すべてのプログラム」に並びます。 通知領域 : Linux のトレイアイコン（StatusNotifierItem と XEmbed）が XP の通知領域に出ます。
XP 自身のネットワーク・バッテリー・音量のアイコンと、そのフライアウト（音量、電源メーター、ワイヤレス ネットワーク接続の狀態）も
出ます。NetworkManager と PipeWire / PulseAudio の狀態から作ります（ AshesTom さんのフォーク の XP Explorer から）。
ワイヤレス ネットワークの一覧から、初めてのネットワークにも XP のネットワーク キーの畫面で接続できます。メニューや畫面の文字は ISO の XP のファイルから読みます。 XP Explorer からの追加 : フォルダの左のタスク ペイン、畫面のプロパティ（Windows XP とクラシックのテーマ、スタイルと配色。
配色は ISO の HIVEDEF.INF と themeui.dll から作ります）、畫像の縮小版とプレビュー、XP のサウンド（起動、ログオン、ログオフも）、
ネットワーク接続、Internet Explorer 6、Windows Media Player 9、スタートメニューの左の列（インターネット、電子メール、
よく使うプログラム）。どれもお手元の ISO のファイルで動きます（ prefix/extras.py ）。 キーボードの配列 : 最初は Linux のシステムの配列（ localectl ）です。コントロール パネルの「地域と言語のオプション」→
「言語」→「詳細」（XP 自身のもの）で入力言語を足したり既定を変えたりすると、セッションの配列（Wayland では labwc、
X11 では setxkbmap）がすぐに従います。2 つ以上なら XP と同じ左 Alt+Shift で切り替わります（ session/keyboard.py ）。 日本語入力 : fcitx5 + Mozc です。Ctrl+Space（または全形/半形）で切り替えます。GTK、Qt、Wine のアプリで使えます。 日本語版と英語版の XP : どちらの ISO でも動きます。言語は ISO から自動で判斷し、字型（英語版は Tahoma など）、

インストーラーが作るショートカットは XP のスタートメニューに入ります。 XP のようこそ畫面 : LightDM の greeter として、XP のようこそ畫面とログオフの畫面を出せます（任意）。

動かすセッションです（XP、ReactOS、Windows 7 のシェル）。モニターごとの倍率や 125%・150% などの倍率が使え、シェルはぼけずに描かれます。

ふだん試すなら X11 のセッションをおすすめします。 ReactOS のシェル（任意） : XP の ISO の代わりに ReactOS 0.4.16 の explorer で動かすセッションです。日本語と英語に対応します。
XP のシェルと並べて入れられます。 Windows 7 のシェル（任意・実験的） : Windows 7 SP1 x64 の explorer で動かすセッションです（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目。
Aero のガラスはまだありません）。スタートメニュー、タスクバー、通知領域、フォルダの窓が動き、Linux のアプリもアプリごとに
タスクバーにまとまります。確かめたのは日本語版と、その文字を英語の言語パックのものに入れ替えた英語版です。 XP のクラシック（ --theme classic ） ReactOS のシェル（ --shell reactos 。XP の ISO は要りません） Windows 7 のシェル（ --shell win7 。実験的） タスクバーの「小さいアイコンを使う」と「結合しない」（すぐに切り替わります） Windows 7 のログオン畫面（ --greeter ） 試してみる Windows XP Professional SP3（x86）の ISO（日本語版か英語版）を ご自身で 用意してください。 新しくインストールした Debian 13 に、ログインして使う利用者として入り、次を実行します。 git clone https://github.com/mikuta0407/win4wine.git ~ /win4wine cd ~ /win4wine

title: Show HN: An agent skill that optimizes code with falsifiable hypotheses
abstract: Hi all, I am a professor in algorithm engineering. In our field we use a method of falsifiable hypothesis testing to improve algorithms. More precisely, this is a cycle consisting of designing an algorithm, analyzing the algorithm, then implementing it and lastly testing it using experiments on real-world instances which leads to designing new algorithms based on the current observations. We put this methodology into an AI skill which runs in an infinite loop. This skill first creates a performance profile, then produces a hypothesis which is implemented and tested automatically using an AI agent. If the change improved the performance and tests negotiated with the user verify it, the change is kept, if not it is discarded. Everything is tracked via version control. Part of the output is a pdf report which documents all the code changes and progress over time as well as individual patches to only merge specific patches if one chooses to do so. Moreover, this comes with a knowledge-base in which we collect global optimization knowledge, thereby improving the skill over time. We ran this on a wide range of public code bases, e.g. our KaHIP graph partitioning toolkit, which improved running time by 3.9x, or our VieCut minimum cut solver, where the skill improved the running time of the system by 8.9x; I do believe the skill is very easy to use and hence am sharing this here. Let me know what you think!

title: Canada recommits to federal funding for news
abstract:
All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites. Nearly there — check your email. We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder. The new budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.” A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again. That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament . With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to. Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan , president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada . The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act , Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.” I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news? “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan said. “They see what Big Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.” There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a new tax credit in California . But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism. The labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year . The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026. “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan said. There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year. “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.” In the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers. But News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms . The Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Launched in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas . The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada. Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results showed the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles. “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities. Many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.” “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he said. Some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted. Deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada , or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media . These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit. “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said. The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics. “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan said. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.” The Cornell Daily Sun saw traffic spike by almost 500% in September. And at Cambridge Day, "having full-time reporters was transformative." Our latest traffic rankings for nonprofit news outlets.
