title: What Happened to Silicon Valley?
abstract:
What Happened to Silicon Valley? From value creation to value extraction By Tim O’Reilly November 20, 2026 • 32 minute read On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years. As delivered, I departed significantly from the script, as you can see from the embedded video below or the transcript that you can see at the link above. It’s an honor to give a lecture in Margaret Levi’s name. I’ve been asked to reflect on the changes in the political economy of Silicon Valley throughout my 40-plus year career in and about it, and I can’t imagine a better framing for my remarks than Margaret’s vision. Margaret understood that advances in our ability to work together are essential to a better future. Cooperation is the human superpower. She also asks what happens when the systems of cooperation we have constructed over time stop holding up their end of the bargain. That is very much the question that Silicon Valley is facing today. An industry that pioneered advances in collective intelligence at scale used to engender love from its customers because of the way it solved new problems in their lives. It now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong? The web I thought we were building in 1993 But let me start with my own history. I started my company more than 40 years ago with a $500 initial investment. We took in no venture capital, and we built a business that now generates hundreds of millions of dollars in profitable annual revenue, funded by customers who love our products and pay us for them. We got there the slow way, through steady organic growth. That is quite anathema to the rush to the top of whatever appears to be the latest hill that seems to characterize Silicon Valley today. Even when climbing that hill traps a company at a local maximum, the hope is to get to payday before the industry moves on to the next hill. My original corporate goal was stated as simply “Interesting work for interesting people.” That evolved into two principles: “Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators,” and “Create more value than you capture.” Those principles shaped not only my company but what I expected the internet to be. When we launched GNN , the Global Network Navigator, in 1993, it was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the World Wide Web, and for two years it was the place people went to find other sites. What we built was a machine for pointing you at the best of what other people had made, and then getting out of your way. Even our idea of advertising was not what you think of today. It was inspired by direct mail advertising, where you’d read articles in a print magazine or look at accompanying ads, and then you’d call an 800 number or circle a number on a “bingo card” that you’d send in to the publisher so that the advertiser could send you a brochure. I realized that the web would be a good replacement for that awkward system, that every company ought to have its own website that provided more information about its products and services. What we invented was not the “grab your attention” kind of advertising. It was all about utility, and sharing information that customers really wanted and needed. In short, it was the commercial web, which no one any longer thinks of as advertising, even though it is the most durable and useful kind. The commercial web was only a small part of what the web became. The web was the playground of amateurs, not entrepreneurs. It was a marvelous collective work of human imagination, creativity, sharing, and ultimately (though that became toxic only later), competition for attention. Our hand-curated catalog of the best websites was soon surpassed by algorithmic solutions like those provided by Google. The amount of content produced was far larger than purely human curation could manage. It was an early example of what Richard Sutton was later to call “the bitter lesson” in his analysis of AI training. In my 2005 essay “ What Is Web 2.0? ” I described how the companies that survived the dotcom bust had all, in one way or another, figured out how to help people navigate the resulting information explosion at scale. As Herbert Simon noted in 1971, an abundance of information leads to a scarcity of attention. In the face of increasing information abundance, he predicted that we would use machines to help us better allocate our time and attention. And so it has transpired: Information has become so abundant that it defies manual curation. Instead, powerful, proprietary algorithmic systems use the data they collect to match users with the answers, news, entertainment, products, applications, and services they seek. Today’s AI is in many ways a continuation of this arc. I called this “harnessing collective intelligence.” All of it was, in economic terms, a set of remarkable advances in networked, data-enabled market coordination. It felt like a public good even when it was privately owned. Hal Varian, formerly Google’s chief economist, once told me that only about 6% of Google search result pages carry any advertising or are otherwise monetized by Google. The other 94% were served up by search in a glorious demonstration of abundance, the surplus of value created over value captured. And while many of the pages themselves were commercial, even more were the product of the joyful exuberance of humanity, people creating and sharing for the joy of it. Google’s algorithm matched that creation to the people who wanted it, with no price involved anywhere in the transaction. Forty thousand times a second, Google’s organic search algorithms were performing the coordination that twentieth-century economists thought could only be done by self-interested actors haggling over prices. And for Google’s first decade and a half, the priced market of advertising ran alongside organic search as a sidecar, not the engine. That’s the Silicon Valley I signed up for. Some of this is nostalgia. The early web had plenty wrong with it, its share of greedy hustlers and hypesters. But value creation for both users and suppliers was the winning strategy. Companies won by solving real problems for their customers. Investors won when the company delivered on their promises. Unfortunately, that didn’t last. The turn to the dark side Google, a company once known for “Don’t be evil,” now faces the same surveillance-capitalism charges as Facebook, a company that never made any such promise. On Google, advertising now pushes organic search far down the page. Especially on mobile, you often scroll through pages of ads from national chains before you reach the site that has the best answer to your question. And in today’s AI-mode search, even the content is served up directly by Google, with far less traffic sent on to the sites that provide it. Likewise, Amazon, which used to call itself the most customer-centric company on earth, now puts sixteen ads and four organic results on a typical search results page. Sometimes, it may take scrolling past three screens of results to reach the first organic search result. And by “the first organic search result,” I mean “the best guess of the company’s smartest algorithms for what the user is actually looking for.” In former times, that was the top result. No more. The reason isn’t that good people turned bad. It’s in the overriding economic incentives of today’s shareholder capitalism. The extractive behavior the tech giants exhibit has been the norm for modern companies since Milton Friedman reset its objective in 1970, in a sentence that became doctrine: “ The social responsibility of business is to increase its profits .

title: The short age of dragon riders
abstract:
Context Since approximately August of this year, the AI models available to the public have passed a threshold: in a proper harness, they are stronger than most theoretical physicists (myself included) at most technical tasks. What counts as “technical” exactly is blurry (and likely to expand) but I take it to include the bulk of what junior theoretical physicists were doing day to day during their PhDs. Concretely, the models are now able to carry out complex analytical calculations, work out lengthy proofs, turn well-posed problems into code, all with minimal input. They iterate, correct their errors, launch simulations to verify their conjectures, and summarize their work. On my own problems, I have already seen the impossible being done several times, starting with Fable 5 in May (I reported some on X and LinkedIn ). Those who deny this progress have just not tried hard enough (with the latest models), or are blinded by their ego. As of November 2026, the best public models still lack research taste. They execute beautifully when given a clear goal but are worse than the best researchers at coming up with good questions, or at having the sparks of creativity needed to get out of a dead end. They do not have as much vision as the best humans. This situation is unlikely to persist. Even if the whole internet has been exhausted to pre-train models, the availability of human data is no longer the bottleneck. Thanks to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), models can improve simply by solving new tasks, and are in no way bound by human intelligence. At least in the immediate future, progress is thus predictable. First, the internal models at OpenAI and Anthropic have now solved countless open problems, showing that they are indeed a generation ahead of what the public currently has access to (which is already superhuman at many tasks). Second, computing power, the only bottleneck, has been increasing steadily, far beyond what was used to train the current best models. Unless the scaling laws surprisingly break down, we have two generations of improvements ahead of us without doing anything new. On top of this, recursive self-improvement is under way, at least in the weak sense that strong models already substantially help design the training environments of their successors. In a nutshell, as long as the datacenters survive kinetic strikes or a grassroots Butlerian Jihad, progress is not going to stop. Like most scientists, I am conflicted. All the friction is gone; problems melt before we can even understand the solution. It is great, and also scary, leading some in the community to hate the models. I have always been a techno-optimist absolutist. It would be a betrayal to flip now that the wave of progress touches my craft. No, even if it burns me, I still think we should steal the fire! Granted, the fire, this time, may come with existential risks for humanity. I think these risks are real, and to leading order, better understood by the nerds in Silicon Valley than by skeptics like Yann LeCun. Alignment research is certainly important, and if slowing down training helps reduce existential risk, then we probably should. But I think it is too easy to reject AI progress for wrong, self-serving reasons, under the guise of a legitimate concern for mankind. And thus, while one should take these risks seriously, it is important to also think about what is left for us in case they are solved. It is still too difficult for me to envision what the steady state may look like, or whether there will even be one. But I would like to discuss what I think we should do (or at least what I am doing) during the transient period of symbiotic human-AI discovery. Grief The first step is to quickly go through the five stages of grief. Mathematicians, as Sylvia Serfaty recently noted in her talk at the IHP , at least seem to have gone through the denial phase. Physicists are likely only three months behind. Prominent mathematicians, even those who were dismissing AI only three months ago, are no longer denying its power. However, the most visible public reaction, initiated by 25 Fields medalists , is terrible in a way that can only be explained by shock. The best problem solvers alive are now claiming that results, proofs, technical breakthroughs, which in many cases gave them their status and fame, were not really the goal. The goal was the friends we made along the way: the serendipitous discoveries, the mathematical community that got built, the long hours spent pondering in front of a blackboard. This enjoyment, this human understanding, for the community and by the community, is what had value all along. I disagree. I think we deserve all the bad things that will happen to us if we react like such sore losers. Serendipitous discoveries are important, but first, it is unclear that AIs will necessarily lead to fewer, and second, the end results clearly mattered and still matter. Seeing the process as an end in itself, rather than a means to an end, is profoundly self-serving, and sadly typical of academia. We have to accept that many things we were doing, sometimes with joy, are already gone. I have spent days massaging an equation to bring it into a form that worked, proud of my virtuosity. I have made complicated calculations with pen and paper, covering entire notebooks to get an answer I could trust. I have spent weeks turning computations into code, and optimized the implementation over months, to be the first to extract certain results from theory. I have fine-tuned plots for hours until they looked pretty. Science was slow; all these steps were important and had to be taught. They were sometimes tedious, sometimes meditative, and tied to our identity. I was good at this, and enjoyed at least a fraction of it. But even if the models do not make any progress, which as I argued is highly unlikely, this is gone . Spending too much time on what is gone will soon be unprofessional, like bringing a coloring book to work. The temptation of vegan science Since AI is now needed to push the frontier of research and understanding, those who do not want to use it sometimes argue that the output of research is researchers themselves (and not so much the results they produce). Hugo Duminil-Copin, a French Fields medalist, explains ( in a recent talk at the Société Mathématique de France ) that no one really cares about or understands his proofs outside of a few experts (which is mostly true, although I personally enjoyed his lectures as a non-expert). As a result, he concludes, his main value for society lies in showing how far the human mind can be pushed with sustained effort and dedication. Hugo Duminil-Copin is an athlete of the mind, an example for the rest of society. If this is true, then indeed Duminil-Copin can never be replaced by AI, and he is right not to use AI too much. He has said he will digest the AI proofs to understand them and pass them on, a bit like chess players studying engine lines, while continuing his own research without AI. Machines may progress to the point where this view (which I find self-serving) is the only reasonable one. But during the transient, I cannot accept it. At least after they are done with their PhDs, researchers are no longer the product of research; what matters is what they do. I hold the naive view that the goal of research is to push toward new results, knowledge, applications, understanding that can be shared. Discoveries are usually a good thing, actually. I think there will still be joy in discoveries even if it is not only humans that push them. If the old ways are gone, at least I want to push to the stars! Riding the dragon As long as there are problems to solve, and as long as we bring something to their resolution, I think we should ride the AI dragon. We should enhance ourselves, move up in abstraction, and let the dragon deal with what it does better than us.

title: Becoming a Magician
abstract:
When I was a teenager I often used fantasy as a vehicle for escapism. Some people, when they fantasise, think about sex or dragons or wildly unlikely events like winning the lottery. I fantasised about things like having a family of twelve children, designing my own octagonal house and being an adult artist who lived with her friends. The last one morphed one day into a detailed imagining of myself as an adult, in a way that seemed incomprehensibly beautiful and liberated to fourteen year old me. Things like living with friends I cared about, having multiple partners who cared about each other, riding my bike everywhere, and making a living as an artist seemed as unattainable as slaying dragons might’ve for teenage boys. The description was about five or six handwritten pages long, and at the time, it was a manifestation of desperate longing to be somewhere other than where I was, someone who felt free and cared for. At the time I saw that description as basically an impossibility; my life could never be so amazing in reality. Fast forward about seven or ten years and I rediscovered the description when I was moving old notebooks and journals from one dusty storage spot to another. As I read through it, I discovered that 90% of the statements I had made in that description were true (or true in spirit). While I didn’t technically live with my partner, he stayed over most days and was close friends with all of my housemates. At the time I was throwing weekly dinner parties where friends would invite random newcomers to attend and I never knew how many people were coming until we actually sat down to eat. Some statements were true down to the suburb I lived in. As I read through the piece with the eyes of 24-year-old me, I felt that it captured with extreme precision the way my life was at that moment. I should point out that after I wrote it, I didn’t ever look back on it. I basically wrote it and then stuffed the notebook in a drawer somewhere and forgot about it. It was incredible to me, despite all the changes that had happened in my life since when I wrote the passage, that I had basically become the person whose life I had dreamed of living as a teenager. That’s pretty fucking cool. But what I realised was that while that vision had been compelling up until that point (24 or 25), in the literal sense of having compelled me forward through life, my fantasies had changed and expanded in the intervening time. If I read that description at 24 as something to aim towards I would have felt bored. Feeling free, loved, cared for, and able to express myself artistically? Sure, that was great. But I felt then (and feel now) that that is a solid baseline for my current adult life – that I would in fact find it surprising if I went for longer than, say, three months without any one of those needs being met. So the challenge now is to write a new version of this fantasy that describes the version of myself that currently feels impossible, and then simply orient myself towards that until it becomes true. … Not only is any sufficiently advanced technology indistinguishable from magic; any sufficiently advanced technologist seems like a magician. In order to write the new version of this life description, I need to imagine a version of myself who, by definition, I cannot understand. If I understood her she wouldn’t be magical. … For several years I competed in bodypainting at the highest level of competition in the world. Every year I would fly to Austria and compete in the World Championships and by the latter years I would consistently rank in the top four or five. This wasn’t unusual; I was aiming for first place and never got it, but most of the time I understood pretty concretely what a first place piece would look like. It felt like incremental improvements from where I was at that point; faster painting, more detailed realism; a competent assistant, some element of luck in how my presentation was perceived by the judges and how everyone else performed that year. I knew the styles, strengths and weaknesses of the other people who consistently ranked in the top ten pretty intimately; I often predicted accurately whether they would move up or down in the rankings each year. You could say that my model of ‘how to succeed at a bodypainting competition’ was technically sufficient, and the thing I needed to work on was merely fine-tuning all the pieces until I ranked higher than everyone else one year. And then came Sanatan Dinda. An Indian visual artist from Kolkata, he didn’t even make the finals the first year he competed, and the next year he placed second with a style that broke half a dozen of the implicit rules of ‘good artwork’ at the competition. He used a monochromatic or even black and white palette. His pieces weren’t flashy, sparkly, or even very ‘pretty’ in a standard sense. He left vast parts covered in brown, or muddy purple, or some other unappealing background colour. But yet the third year he came he won the entire competition by something like ten percent of the total awarded points over the next artist in second place. His first piece brought people to tears. It was brutal and glorious and technical perfection, but not just that. There was some sort of soul in it that suddenly made all the other bodypaint works seem lacking. His second piece did something similar. I didn’t win that year (obviously; he did) but I didn’t even mind because I was so glad that work like his existed and that the World Bodypainting Festival had, in some way, helped facilitate that art existing. The thing that confused me though was this – I could not work out how he did it. Like, I had zero mental model of how he created that piece in the same timeframe we all had; how he came up with it, designed it, practiced it. Even though he placed first and I placed fifth and logically we both existed on a scale of ‘competence at bodypainting’ it seemed like the skills required were completely different. You could not simply scale up my abilities and get Sanatan’s. You would have had to step back and build something completely different altogether. When I speak to Sanatan (I haven’t picked his brain relentlessly, but I have asked him a bunch of questions when I’ve had the chance) I don’t get any closer to a mental model that would allow me to paint like that. It seems to require completely different mental inputs entirely. The feeling I get, as a very good bodypainter looking at Sanatan’s work, is that I am looking at magic. And that, in fact, is my definition of magic – competence so much more advanced than yours with such alien mental models that you cannot predict the outcomes of the model at all. If you asked me to imitate the work of any of the top 20 bodypainters, I could give you a fair imitation, given enough time and access to reference images. With his work I have no idea. And yet, ten years ago when I encountered the website of the World Bodypainting Festival, as not-yet-a-bodypainter, literally every image on the website was in that category for me. I look at those pieces now and could replicate any of them, but at the time they seemed incredibly complex, technical and inscrutable – I couldn’t break down what steps the artist might have taken or why. I just saw them as unattainable. … One of my heuristics for growth is to seek out the magicians, and find the magic. Often without noticing, your progress in aspects of life or all of it unconsciously becomes linear. You made a certain amount of money last year, so you aim to make some ‘reasonable’ proportion more this year. But you are largely using the same tools to get 2x as you used to get x, and so you end up with diminishing marginal returns as you wring the remaining juice out of the initial strategy.

title: One man's quest to end daylight savings
abstract:
Save this story Save this story Save this story Save this story You’re reading The Talk of the Town : fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond. At a rally in Mississippi not long ago, Donald Trump complained about the reason for his frequent tardiness. “I’m always late. You know, I had a big meeting and I was an hour late. I said, ‘How?’ ” he told the crowd. “Daylight-saving time. We change it twice a year. . . . It’s ridiculous.” Trump has been urging the Senate to approve the Sunshine Protection Act—which was passed by the House in July and would make daylight-saving time permanent—before the bill expires at the end of the current Congress, on January 3rd. His speech recalled an episode of HBO’s “Veep” in which Congressman Jonah Ryan is two hours late to a meeting after adjusting his clock the wrong way. “That’s impossible,” Ryan says. “I set my watch back for daylight-savings time. I springed backwards!” Told that he should have sprung forward, he’s irate: “Have you ever watched girls’ gymnastics? That makes no sense!” “It’s a naturally funny topic,” Scott Yates said late last month, the day before the clocks were set back. Yates, a sixty-one-year-old former journalist, has spent a decade trying to end the changing of the clocks. “Some people plan their vacations around golf,” he said. “I use frequent-flier miles to fly to Michigan to testify.” He was sitting outside a former chapel in Liberia, Costa Rica, to which he relocated from Colorado, in 2024. The country does not change the clocks. “It’s not the No. 1 reason I moved here, but it’s on the list,” he said. He wore Birkenstocks and no watch. Yates began his crusade after he read the book “ A Complaint Free World .” “The idea is, if you can’t do something about it, you shouldn’t complain about it,” he said. “Robbing an hour of sleep just always annoyed me.” So he started a blog (locktheclock.net) in which he compiles research on the topic. Yates found that studies linked the “spring forward” clock change—where people lose an hour of sleep—to a rise in heart attacks and medical incidents involving human error, while the “fall backward” clock change—where it gets dark earlier—led to an increase in fatal auto accidents. Both changes are associated with a spike in strokes. “They’re trying to cut costs by combining Employee of the Month with Flavor of the Month.” Cartoon by Mike Twohy Copy link to cartoon Copy link to cartoon Link copied Shop Shop Within a couple of years, legislators in more than a dozen states started contacting Yates about his writing. He’s helped draft bills, spoken at hearings, and, last year, testified before the Senate Commerce Committee, advocating to end clock changing. (His proposal would give states two years to decide which time to lock in.) He concluded his testimony with a story about how scientists often avoid changing lab rats’ schedules after a clock change because it disrupts results. “At long last, can we treat our citizens with the decency that we treat our lab rats?” he asked the senators. Yates often gets e-mails from people with their own ideas about how to solve the problem. Computer programmers reach out suggesting that we stop using time zones and time changes altogether and put the whole world on Coördinated Universal Time, the international time standard. In New York, this might mean waking up at noon and having lunch at 6 P.M. “It’s never going to happen,” Yates said. The idea of daylight-saving time was first implemented in Germany during the First World War, to save on energy costs, but it had built steam earlier in Europe as a health movement and was helped along by a golf-loving Englishman named William Willett, who liked to go riding early in the morning. “He was me a hundred years earlier,” Yates said. In 1907, Willett distributed a pamphlet called “The Waste of Daylight,” promoting a plan for four twenty-minute advances in the clock throughout the year. It went nowhere. Around the same time, the National Baseball League wanted more light for evening games, while movie-theatre executives wanted less, thinking that darkness might drive people into cinemas. In the states, daylight-saving time was implemented as a fragmented system throughout the World Wars and assorted energy crises. In New York City, in 1951, Grand Central Terminal was home to two railroads that used different times. In the early sixties, there were twenty-three different combinations of start and end dates for daylight-saving time in Iowa alone. The Times described it as “time schizophrenia.” To remedy the clock anarchy, the Uniform Time Act of 1966 standardized the dates for daylight-saving time and gave states the option of moving to permanent Standard Time. Only Hawaii, Arizona (except the Navajo Nation), Puerto Rico, and a few other U.S. territories do not change the clocks. “Time doesn’t exist,” Yates said. “The thing that we call time is just what we all agree on.” The Sunshine Protection Act is the closest he has come to getting his way, but the House bill is slightly different than what he advocated for. “Washington is just so dysfunctional,” he said. “If this was a thing with money behind it, it would’ve been worked out.” He added, “I’m so worried about Trump being in favor of it, because I don’t want to ruin it for another fifty years.” ♦

title: What we learned operating auth for 1k APIs
abstract:
In May 2025, we merged a PR at Nango that had a critical bug: an if condition that never fired prevented refreshed credentials from being saved to the database. We caught the bug and reverted it in just under two hours. In those two hours, our scheduled jobs had refreshed and discarded access and refresh tokens for hundreds of connections. For most APIs, that was recoverable: the old refresh token still worked, so the next scheduled refresh repaired the connection. Then we learned how many providers rotate refresh tokens. Many providers, including Airtable and Atlassian, invalidate the old refresh token the moment a replacement is issued. Salesforce and Slack can do the same when rotation is enabled for the OAuth app. There was no way to get those tokens back. For every affected connection, our customers had to ask their users to go through the consent screen again. OAuth is a standard, but OAuth providers are not interchangeable. Each API’s auth behaves a little differently, and some of those differences are undocumented and only surface in production. For context, Nango is an open-source project that lets web applications and agents integrate with third-party APIs. Our customers embed it in their products. Their users connect third-party accounts, and Nango keeps those connections working. Since then, we’ve grown from supporting about 400 APIs to 1,500+ APIs. The incident changed how we operate auth, but it was only the first of several lessons. Lesson 1: Token rotation makes ordinary bugs irreversible Refresh token rotation is a security win, but a bug in the rotation path can permanently destroy a connection and force the user to reauthorize. That’s what made our incident so expensive. We now treat refresh tokens like money, not cache. The new token gets persisted before anything else can fail. The persistence path has its own regression tests, and any platform-level refresh anomalies immediately page the on-call team. Providers enforce refresh-token rotation differently Take Airtable: a refresh request with a stale token or the wrong client credentials can return a 400 or 401, but Airtable doesn’t stop there. It revokes the user’s entire authorization for your app, and the only way back is for the user to reconnect. Sending the same refresh request twice can also cause revocation. Airtable documents a short grace period for duplicate refreshes, but retrying the stale token after that period revokes the authorization. Airtable also invalidates the old access token the instant a refresh succeeds, so a long-running job still using an old token can fail mid-run. Xero handles it better : if a refresh fails or the response never arrives, you can retry with the previous refresh token for up to 30 minutes. Issues like these pushed us to serialize refreshes per connection behind a distributed lock. * This is only the success path. Failure paths don’t fit in one diagram. Even refreshing early can be wrong. For example, Exact Online’s access tokens last for 10 minutes, and its token endpoint rejects any refresh attempt made more than 30 seconds before expiry. Our “refresh 15 minutes early” rule meant every refresh fell outside that window and was rejected. We had to add support for per-provider expiration buffers . Lesson 2: You can’t reliably know when access tokens expire The official OAuth 2.0 spec ( RFC 6749 ) makes expires_in optional for access tokens. For us, this has been a recurring source of silent breakage. Zendesk, for example, rolled out expiring access tokens for OAuth clients, including existing ones. Its token response includes expires_in only if you request it . Without that parameter, the access token still expires under the default policy, but the response doesn’t say when. We discovered this only after the rotating refresh token lapsed and connections started dying. Salesforce’s token response includes no expiry. The documented way to check it is a separate introspection endpoint, which we call before deciding whether to refresh an access token. POST /services/oauth2/introspect HTTP / 1.1 Host : yourInstance.my.salesforce.com Authorization : Basic <base64 of client_id:client_secret> Content-Type : application/x-www-form-urlencoded token=<access_token>&token_type_hint=access_token Sample response: { "active" : true , "scope" : " id api refresh_token " , "exp" : 1549921091 , "iat" : 1549917491 , "token_type" : " Bearer " , "client_id" : " xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx " } But in June 2024, the introspection endpoint started intermittently returning unsupported_token_type for some tokens. When introspection failed, we refreshed anyway. The replacement access token could be introspected normally, though we never learned why the original token failed. Refresh token lifetimes are just as inconsistent NetSuite’s OAuth refresh tokens expire after 7 days , requiring full re-consent, which is why many teams use its token-based authentication instead. Google’s refresh tokens live indefinitely, except under documented conditions , including the app being in “Testing” status, six months without use, or a user exceeding 100 live refresh tokens for your client. We now refresh stale credentials on a cron , so tokens get exercised before inactivity kills them. Auth failures don’t always look like failures You’d expect an auth failure to return a 401. It often doesn’t: Zoho CRM’s token endpoint returns HTTP 200 with the error in the body . Workday and Dayforce return no error at all when a permission policy is missing; the API just returns empty data. One SOAP-based API we support returns HTTP 200 for everything, including wrong passwords. LastPass does the same, with the failure as plain text in the body. Our credential check for it literally searches the response for the string “Authorization Error”. We ended up building per-provider heuristics: at the time of this analysis, 276 of the roughly 935 providers in our registry declared an authenticated endpoint that Nango can call to check whether credentials still work. Lesson 3: Providers make breaking changes to their API auth 16% of commits to our provider config are fixes. There’s no reliable feed for provider auth changes; we often learn about them from a failed flow or a customer report. Figma announced by email that credentials had to move from the request body to a Basic Authorization header and that the OAuth host was changing. We shipped the update , but anyone who missed the email might not discover the change until refreshes begin failing. Shopify changed how offline tokens are issued, so apps began receiving expiring tokens where they previously didn’t. We shipped a config change to preserve the old behavior. Lesson 4: Sometimes you build around the provider, not with it Supporting a new API assumes two things: you can get credentials to test with, and you can find accurate docs for how its auth works. At our scale, both assumptions fail often enough that going around the provider is routine: Salesforce Data Cloud is separately provisioned, and none of our test orgs included it. Its auth requires two chained token exchanges against different hosts. We built a mock server from the documented responses so we could implement and test the flow without live credentials. LastPass’s API isn’t really REST: nearly every operation hits the same URL, with the action passed in the request body. That broke an assumption in our proxy that every integration would define individual endpoints, so we added support for APIs with only a base URL . A community member found the solution to a recurring Asana OAuth error ( client_id is missing or invalid ) in Asana’s support forum and added it to our docs . It wasn’t covered in Asana’s own docs. Read.ai’s documented authorization URL pointed at their internal developer-testing page . The real endpoint came from querying their OpenID discovery endpoint directly.

title: The next circle of security hell
abstract:
A few years back I wrote “The modern packager’s security nightmare” . Have things improved since? On the contrary, I feel like we’re slipping down a well-oiled slope with no end in sight. Vulnerabilities are reported at unprecedented rates. A lot of people are doing everything they can to patch them up, which doesn’t necessarily mean they’re not making things even worse. Complex software involves complex trees of dependencies, and every branch on that tree needs tending to. When they stop being reliable, people further down the tree start taking more weight. And there’s a limit of how much a single person can do, so what started as an effort to resolve an issue upstream may quickly become a weakness. Is software less secure these days? It’s tempting to say yes. I’d love to blame the corporate sector for egotistically dumping low quality software on us. I’d love to blame marketing-oriented people developing stuff with the sole goal of making a profit. I’d love to blame Rust for getting people obsessed about memory safety, and ignoring the kinds of vulnerabilities that aren’t caught by the compiler. Finally, I’d really love to blame slop. But the truth is, I don’t know. That’s really beside the point. The point is that nowadays everyone and their chatbot became security researchers. Projects are being flooded with vulnerability reports. Even though pretty much every bug bounty was discontinued because of slop, people aren’t stopping. And even if we disregard truly invalid junk reports, there’s a lot left, and you have to deal with them somehow. You have to figure out how important they are, and how to fix them (or more likely, whether the fixes submitted are truly valid and don’t introduce regressions), or if you should reject them and why. In the end, security is tricky. We’re seeing lots of bugs like REDoS, or other kinds of “performance bugs”. Are they really vulnerabilities? Well, it depends on the attack vector. And that in turn depends on how the software is used. Some scenarios are really contrived, and feel like “shell can execute dangerous commands if you type them in”. But then, you also have really serious issues such as “timing attack can be used to guess user’s secret”. You need to know a lot to make that kind of judgment, and sometimes your judgment doesn’t really match users’ expectations. In the end, what can project maintainers do? Even if they have the expertise and the energy to judge, if they can “know better”, there’s likely a CVE assigned already. It may have absurdly high score. All security scanners will complain unless you fix it, and users will come asking or complaining, or attacking, or forking. I mean, technology can’t handle nuances. More than once I’ve been doing unnecessary security stabilizations over vulnerabilities that didn’t affect Gentoo (for example, because we already unbundled the vulnerable dependencies), to avoid false positives from security scanners. I’ve been also doing meaningless version bumps (with no real changes or no changes that applied to Gentoo) so that our packages don’t get reported as being “outdated”. It’s a hassle and it sucks, but it saves people from worrying. I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: most projects aren’t really prepared to handle security issues. And it’s not just about triage. It’s about having LTS or security branches, it’s about making proper security releases with minimal changes. Unfortunately, it’s quite common for security fixes to be combined with new features, deprecations, API changes. In extreme cases, people are caught with their metaphorical pants down, and suddenly need to make a security release in the middle of a major rewrite, or along with barely tested new code. And then, people downstream discover that they need to quickly deal with major API changes to upgrade past a vulnerable version. These things keep piling up. What happens next? The community reaches a breaking point. People can’t keep up. You discover you can’t rely on others, so you work around them. You start bundling more stuff. Soon enough your workload goes beyond your ability. Software development becomes “every chatbot for itself”. The nightmare becomes worse, and the wheel keeps turning.

title: Same Code, Different Findings: An Empirical Study of Run-to-Run Instability in Rule-Based and LLM-Based Security Scanners
abstract: Security scanners in CI/CD pipelines are believed to give the same answers for the same code. When a finding disappears, it is treated as fixed, and when a scan stage finds no blocking vulnerabilities, the build proceeds to production. This study tests that assumption. It ran 350 rule-based scans of 12 projects with Opengrep and CodeQL under normal, low-memory and busy-CPU conditions, and scanned 172 labelled cases five times each with four LLMs. For the rule-based scanners, resource budgets silently change the results: in one project, 32% of the findings appear and disappear across runs of the same commit ID. This study shows that when LLM-based scanners are added as a build step in CI/CD, for 3 out of the 4 models, between 28.2% and 91.1% of the findings do not occur across same runs; setting the temperature to 0 reduces but doesn't remove the variation, and new models are no longer accepting a temperature setting. Unstable LLM findings are more likely to be off-target noise, even on novel code. One scan recovers only 39–98% of the findings of five scans, and keeping only findings reported in all five runs raises the share of true positives at almost no loss of recall. Inconsistency means opposite things for the two types of scanners: a lost detection for the rule-based engines and noise for the LLMs. These results call for CI build gates that treat incomplete scans as failures, and for remediation tracking that does not treat a missing finding as a fix.

title: The IGVF Catalog Knowledge Graph
abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) consortium is systematically characterizing how genomic variation influences regulatory elements, gene expression, and human phenotypes through thousands of experimental mapping and perturbation datasets alongside predictive models. To synthesize these diverse results into quantitative relationships and situate them within established biological knowledge, we developed the IGVF Catalog, a large-scale knowledge graph. Implemented in ArangoDB using schema-validated JSON records. Version 1.3 encompasses nearly 3 billion nodes across 14 entity types (including variants, coding variants, genomic elements, genes, transcripts, proteins, pathways, and ontology graphs for biosamples and phenotypes) connected by more than 8.6 billion edges across 31 relationship types. Edges encode statistical significance, effect sizes, source provenance, and biological context via ontology-linked hyperedges. The Catalog integrates 657 IGVF datasets spanning non-coding reporter and CRISPR perturbation screens (MPRA, STARR-seq, Perturb-seq), coding variant assays (VAMP-seq, SGE, MAVE, DUAL-IPA), and predictive models (scE2G, SEMVAR, cV2F, TLAND, and BlueSTARR), unified with extensive public context including GENCODE annotations, FAVOR and dbSNP variants, TopLD linkage disequilibrium, GWAS, QTLs, and protein interactions. Users can interrogate the Catalog through a web portal (https://catalog.igvf.org), Python and R clients, an OpenAPI-documented API featuring 86 endpoints supporting identifier and genomic-region queries, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enabling agent-assisted querying with large language models. We demonstrate the Catalog’s utility for mechanistic interpretation across three case studies: resolving a FOXA1-dependent enhancer variant (rs11257655) regulating CAMK1D at a type 2 diabetes locus, distinguishing coding (GCKR rs1260326) and regulatory (HNF1A rs1169289) mechanisms for liver traits, and linking vascular CRISPRi-perturbed elements to CDKN2A/CDKN2B and NOS3 in coronary artery disease. Updated quarterly with open data and software, the IGVF Catalog provides a scalable resource for variant-to-function discovery.

title: Monitorable-by-design architectures for a post-Astra world: a compartmentalization-based approach
abstract: Frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are increasingly able to do substantial reasoning without a monitorable chain of thought, chains of thought are becoming less legible, and are often monitored asynchronously to reduce cost. With the future of chain of thought monitoring unclear, it may be necessary to design LLMs with monitorability in mind. We propose a modification to existing LLM architectures based on GRAM, SGTM, DEMix, BTS, and similar methods to compartmentalize dangerous capabilities so that their use, especially in combination with dangerous reasoning types that may indicate strategic adversarial use, can be monitored more cheaply than chain of thought in a way that might outlast monitorable chain of thought. We propose several variants of this architecture designed to balance tradeoffs and discuss other benefits, such as capability removal.

title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.

title: A Knowledge-Augmented Large Language Model for Power System Security Risk Reasoning
abstract: With the increasing complexity of modern power systems caused by renewable energy integration, distributed energy resources, and cyber–physical interactions, accurate and trustworthy security risk reasoning has become increasingly important. Existing data-driven methods mainly focus on risk prediction based on statistical correlations, while lacking the capability to model causal risk evolution and generate interpretable explanations. This paper proposes a knowledge-augmented large language model framework for power system security risk reasoning (KALLM-PSR). The proposed framework integrates structured power system knowledge with large language model reasoning capabilities to construct knowledge-enhanced representations, perform multi-stage risk propagation analysis, and generate reliability-aware explanations. A consistency evaluation mechanism is further introduced to improve the trustworthiness of reasoning results. Extensive experiments on IEEE 14-bus, 39-bus, and 118-bus systems demonstrate that KALLM-PSR outperforms conventional deep learning models, general large language models (LLMs), and retrieval-augmented approaches in risk identification accuracy, reasoning consistency, explanation quality, and robustness under disturbance conditions. The proposed framework provides an effective approach for intelligent and trustworthy power system security management.

title: Mining and Automating Expert Guidance in Open Source: A Multi-Agent Framework Informed by the PyTorch Community
abstract: The continuous participation of newcomers is critical to the sustainability of Open Source Software (OSS) communities, yet many face technical and social challenges in making their first contributions. Expert guidance can help newcomers navigate these challenges, but timely support is not consistently available. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer potential to augment this support, existing models lack project-specific context and awareness of mentoring practices. To investigate these challenges, we analyze OSS expert–newcomer interactions by curating 383 dialogues from Good First Issues (GFIs) in the PyTorch repository. We directly observe that interactions are typically brief, over one-third of newcomer inquiries remain unanswered, and the median first response time is 6.3 hours, revealing gaps and delays in expert involvement. From these interactions, we derive a taxonomy of 50 recurring, context-dependent expert guidance strategies across 11 themes, grounded in prior OSS mentoring research. Building on these findings, we introduce StrategicMentor, a strategy-driven multi-agent framework that integrates strategy knowledge with project, task, and dialogue context to deliver personalized, context-aware guidance. Coordinating specialized LLM-based agents via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the framework operationalizes these strategy patterns without reproducing every raw expert reply or the limitations of the existing process. In our user study, StrategicMentor received higher ratings than the baseline LLM and sampled human expert responses across the evaluated dimensions and was generally preferred by both newcomers and experienced contributors. This work contributes a publicly available Expert–Newcomer dialogue dataset, a structured characterization of OSS mentoring strategies, and a multi-agent framework for investigating scalable, expert-informed onboarding support in OSS communities.

title: Delving into Decline: The Rise and Fall of Large Language Model Vocabulary in Biomedical Abstracts, 2018–2026
abstract: Style words such as delve, intricate and meticulous became several times more frequent in English research abstracts after large language models became public. Publicly named as evidence of machine-assisted writing, they have since turned down as a set. The prevailing explanation, deliberate avoidance, predicts that the words named most widely receded furthest, a prediction tested here on every eligible PubMed abstract entered from January 2018 to June 2026 (N = 10,767,846). Thirty such words were compared by segmented regression against two control sets from the same corpus: comparably frequent words that never rose, and emphatic markers from a published metadiscourse inventory. Lexical density, nominalisation, passive voice and hedging were also measured. How widely each word had been named was scored beforehand across fourteen independent inventories. Twenty-nine of the thirty turned down and neither control set did, ruling out corpus drift and a general cooling of evaluative prose. Public naming did not predict the decline to the extent the awareness account requires: a word’s earlier rise predicted its fall, naming added nothing with that rise held constant, and the steepest decliners include words on no inventory. The structural features did not turn back. The test is powered to detect an association of the size that account requires, not a weak one, which cannot be excluded. Model turnover or heavier editing of output fits the pattern better than selective avoidance; these data cannot separate them. The visible lexical signal of machine-assisted writing is weakening; the impersonal texture of the prose is not.

title: Sentence Boundary Detection in Colloquial Tamil Using Monolingual Adaptation and Fine-Tuned mBART50
abstract: Sentence boundary detection is an essential preprocessing task that converts continuous text into sentence-level units for downstream natural language processing applications. It is particularly challenging in colloquial text, where punctuation is inconsistent and informal expressions differ from standard written forms. This study investigates a sequence-to-sequence approach to sentence boundary detection in colloquial Tamil using mBART50. In the first stage, the pretrained model is adapted using approximately 5,700 monolingual colloquial Tamil sentences, reducing perplexity from 2.7859 to 2.2857. In the second stage, a separate segmentation dataset is prepared by recombining sentences into synthetic paragraph examples containing two to five sentences. These examples are shuffled and used for mixed-difficulty supervised fine-tuning. The proposed configuration achieves a boundary-level precision of 0.8169, recall of 0.8506, and F1-score of 0.8334. The findings indicate the potential of monolingual adaptation for this task under the prepared evaluation setting. However, evaluation on larger, independently sourced conversational Tamil data is needed to assess performance on naturally occurring text.

title: AI-Based Research Paper Analysis and Assistance System
abstract: The growing volume of scholarly publications makes it difficult for students and early-stage researchers to examine every paper in depth. This paper presents an AI-based research paper analysis and assistance system that supports the initial examination of research articles through three integrated functions: paper summarization, AI-assisted research-gap suggestions, and context-based question answering. The application accepts a research paper in PDF format, extracts its machine-readable text, performs basic text preparation, and submits the processed content to the Google Gemini large language model (LLM) for task-specific analysis. A Streamlit interface provides access to the analysis functions, while Supabase supports user authentication and paper-history management. Python, pypdf, NLTK, and environment-based configuration are used in the implementation. The system is intended to help users locate key information and develop an initial understanding of a paper; it does not replace close reading, systematic literature review, or expert assessment. The current implementation is text-oriented and may not fully interpret figures, equations, scanned pages, or very long documents. Since no controlled benchmark or user study is reported in the present implementation, the results are discussed in terms of implemented functionality rather than quantitative performance. The paper describes the system architecture, processing workflow, implementation choices, observed capabilities, limitations, and directions for further development.

title: The new production logic? Exploring human-AI creative workflows in China’s video game development
abstract:
China’s rapidly expanding video game sector has become a key site of AI-driven industrial transformation. The integration of AI is reshaping video game development through the emergence of human–AI collaborative workflows.
 Drawing on the Frankfurt School’s critical theory of the culture industry, this study examines how generative AI is reshaping production processes and creative labour practices across the pre-production, production, and post-production stages of China’s video game industry. Based on semi-structured interviews with game professionals from major Chinese game studios, the study finds that AI integration reinforces the industrialisation and standardisation of cultural production, particularly through enhanced workflow efficiency and quality control. At the same time, it reconfigures creative labour by shifting workers’ responsibilities towards directing, supervising, and evaluating AI-assisted production processes. These developments illustrate the dual implications of AI adoption: while generative AI intensifies technological rationalisation, human creative judgement remains central to ensuring cultural specificity and context-sensitive creative outcomes. The study argues that human labour is not displaced but reconfigured within AI-enabled production, mediating the tension between industrial standardisation and culturally specific forms of video game production.

title: ModernELECTRA: Replaced-Token Detection with Boundary-Window Reconstruction for Compact Encoders that Classify and Embed
abstract: ELECTRA-style replaced-token detection (RTD) is a sample-efficient objective for pre-training text encoders, and RTD-trained models such as DeBERTaV3 are strong on classification benchmarks. The same models, however, are known to be poor backbones for embedding tasks such as retrieval and semantic similarity: the binary"original vs. replaced"signal does not ask the final layer to retain the token identity and contextual content that dense representations rely on. We introduce ModernELECTRA, a pre-training recipe that keeps RTD as the main objective and adds a lightweight auxiliary task, boundary-window reconstruction. For every token, we sample a window of 3-12 tokens that strictly contains it and reconstruct the token's original identity only from the discriminator's hidden states at the two window boundaries. The task costs one small FFN at training time and is discarded afterwards, yet it forces every final-layer state to carry information about its neighbourhood. Combined with a frozen, separately pre-trained generator, a temperature curriculum for hard negatives and a 512-to-8192 length curriculum, we train two compact encoders: EdgeCoder-31M, an 8-layer English model, and EdgeCoder-Multilingual-61M, a 16-layer model covering 46 languages, each on about 1T tokens. They reach 86.0 and 85.1 on GLUE. The English model outperforms Ettin-Enc-32m (83.5) and MiniLM-L12 (84.6) on GLUE while matching them on MTEB English v2 (51.1), and the multilingual model outperforms the 2.3x larger mmBERT-small on GLUE and Multilingual MiniLM and mDistilBERT on XTREME over the languages it covers. We also describe FlashDeBERTa, our open-source fused implementation of DeBERTa's disentangled attention that stores no $n \times n$ score matrix: at 4096 tokens it is 10x faster and uses 93% less memory than the reference implementation, and it loads existing DeBERTa checkpoints unchanged.

title: Digital authoritarianism and generative AI: Comparative perspectives on datafication, control, and manipulation
abstract: Although authoritarian actors have long used advanced technologies for control, manipulation, and repression, GenAI adds a new and consequential layer to digital authoritarianism. The emergence and widespread adoption of generative models provide non-democratic forces with unprecedented tools to develop new tactics to reshape information environments, influence public opinion, and expand systems of surveillance and control. This special theme examines the evolving nexus between GenAI and digital authoritarianism through conceptual, theoretical, empirical, and comparative contributions. The articles explore this relationship across diverse political contexts, including Russia, China, the UK, Turkey, and Tunisia. Methodologically, the special theme brings together a wide range of approaches, strengthening our understanding of how GenAI affects digital authoritarianism at different levels. Finally, it advances knowledge of less explored issues, including how GenAI reinforces authoritarian practices through legal procedures, institutional arrangements, and algorithmic decision-making systems.
